title: Forming nouns
summary: Put ang, ng or sa in front of a verb or adjective and it becomes a noun: the one who, the thing that, what is
goals: Turn a verb or an adjective into a noun with ang, ng or sa
Use ang mga, ng mga and sa mga for plural nouns
Understand the meanings: the one who, the thing that, the one which, what is
Read the book's sample sentences and spot the new nouns

sections.title: Making a noun from a verb or adjective

blocks.t: In Tagalog you can turn a **verb** or an **adjective** into a **noun** very simply: put the article [[ang|marker]] or [[ng|marker]], or the preposition [[sa|marker]], in front of it.
If the noun is **plural**, the little word shows it too: they become [[ang mga|marker]], [[ng mga|marker]] and [[sa mga|marker]] (you met these in Lesson 4).
The verb can be in **any tense**: past, present or future.

blocks.title: ang / ng / sa + verb or adjective = a noun
blocks.note: the one who ate · the one who is good · the poor people · to one who is studying

blocks.title: Think of it like English
blocks.t: English needs extra words to do this: *the one who* ate, *what* I am eating. Tagalog just puts **ang**, **ng** or **sa** in front of the verb or adjective.
The person or thing you are talking about can be **stated**, or it can be left **understood** (implied). Compare these two sentences:

items.tl: Ang kumain ng manggá ay si Jose.
items.en: The one who ate the mango is Jose.

items.tl: Ang batàng kumain ng manggá ay si Jose.
items.en: The child who ate the mango is Jose.

blocks.title: Shorter is better
items: Both sentences are correct, but the **first** one is used more because it is **short** and easy to say.
The second is **redundant**: it mentions **batà** (child), but we already understand the child is Jose.

blocks.t: In each sentence below, the book underlines the **new noun**: the article (ang, ng or sa, with or without mga) plus the verb or adjective. Here they are shown as the coloured noun.

items.tl: Binabása mo ba ang sinulat ko?
items.en: Are you reading what was written by me? (literal)
The one who is speaking is the president.
The one sleeping is like an angel.

items.tl: Masaráp ang mga lúlutuin ko para sa iyó.
items.en: Delicious, what I shall cook for you. (literal) / I shall cook a delicious meal for you.

items.tl: Ang mga sinásabi niyá ay hindî totoó.
items.en: What are said by him/her are not true. (literal) / What he is saying is not true.
I saw what she was reading.
The one who is good has many friends.

items.tl: Ang mga mahihírap ay walang maraming kagamitán.
items.en: The poor people do not have many possessions.
Will not go hungry, the hardworking. (literal) / The hardworking will not go hungry.

items.tl: Nagagálit ang gurò sa mga tamád.
items.en: The teacher is angry with the lazy ones.
He is asking for what I am eating.

items.tl: Naaáwà ako sa mga humíhingî ng pera.
items.en: I pity those who are asking for money.

items.tl: Sa nag-áaral, ang sípag ay kailangan.
items.en: To one who is studying, diligence is necessary.

blocks.title: Two kinds of noun
blocks.t: The last sentence has **two nouns**: **sa nag-áaral** (one who is studying) is made from a **verb**, while **sípag** (diligence) is a **true noun**.

blocks.title: Look closely
items: **ang mga lúlutuin**, **ang mga sinásabi**, **ang mga mahihírap**, **sa mga tamád** and **sa mga humíhingî** are **plural**, so they use **mga**.
In **Humíhingî siyá ng kinakáin ko** the new noun is introduced by **ng**, not ang.
Some sentences sound more natural in a free English translation, so the book gives a literal one and a natural one.

blocks.title: Spelling
items: The vocabulary list writes **sipág** (diligence); the sentence writes **sípag**.
The sample sentence writes **natútulog**; the book's exercise below writes **natutúlog** (as in Lesson 12).

blocks.t: The vocabulary list also gives **pangulo** = president (Lesson 26) and **masípag** = hardworking (Lesson 6 gave it as *industrious*).
The book asks you to **find the nouns** in these sentences, then translate them into Tagalog. It prints no answers. Use the patterns above: ang / ng / sa + verb or adjective.

head: Sentence
rows: The one who arrived was my father.
This will be for the poor.
The one she loves is an intelligent man.
I shall give this to the one who is leaving.
The one which he read was Rizal.
The thing she ate was not good.
The one which is good is the thing I bought.
The expensive one should not be bought.

blocks.t: Then make your own sentences using these phrases as **subjects**, **predicates** or **objects**:

blocks.title: Remember
items: ang / ng / sa + verb or adjective = a noun.
Plural: ang mga, ng mga, sa mga.
The verb can be past, present or future.
The new noun means the one who, the thing that, the one which, or what is.
The person can be stated (ang batàng kumain) or understood (ang kumain); the short way is used more.

exercises.q: How do you turn a verb or adjective into a noun in Tagalog?
options: Put ang, ng or sa in front of it
Put ay in front of it
exercises.answer: Put ang, ng or sa in front of it
exercises.explain: For example ang kumain, the one who ate.
ang + kumain (ate) = the one who ate.

options: ang mga, ng mga, sa mga
ang ang, ng ng, sa sa
exercises.answer: ang mga, ng mga, sa mga

exercises.q: Which tenses can the verb be in?
options: any tense: past, present or future
exercises.answer: any tense: past, present or future
exercises.explain: Ang kumain (past), ang nagsásalitâ (present), ang mga lúlutuin (future).

exercises.q: Which sentence does the book say is used more?
options: Ang kumain ng manggá ay si Jose.
Ang batàng kumain ng manggá ay si Jose.
exercises.answer: Ang kumain ng manggá ay si Jose.
exercises.explain: It is shorter and easier to say.

exercises.q: Why is "Ang batàng kumain ng manggá ay si Jose" called redundant?
options: batà is already understood to be Jose
exercises.answer: batà is already understood to be Jose

exercises.q: What does "Ang nagsásalitâ ay ang pangulo" mean?
options: The one who is speaking is the president.
The one sleeping is like an angel.
exercises.answer: The one who is speaking is the president.
exercises.explain: ang + nagsásalitâ = the one who is speaking.

exercises.q: In "Humíhingî siyá ng kinakáin ko", which word introduces the new noun?
exercises.explain: ng kinakáin ko = what I am eating.

exercises.q: "Sa nag-áaral, ang sípag ay kailangan." Which noun is a TRUE noun?
exercises.explain: sa nag-áaral is a noun formed from a verb; sípag (diligence) is a true noun.

exercises.q: "Naaáwà ako sa mga humíhingî ng pera." Who are sa mga humíhingî?
exercises.explain: I pity those who are asking for money.
Naaáwà ako sa mga humíhingî ng pera.
Nagagálit ang gurò sa mga tamád.

exercises.en: The one who ate the mango is Jose.

recap: Put ang, ng or sa in front of a verb or adjective to make a noun: ang kumain, ng kinakáin, sa nag-áaral.
For plurals use ang mga, ng mga, sa mga: ang mga mahihírap, sa mga tamád.
The verb can be in any tense.
The new noun means the one who, the thing that, the one which, or what is.
The person can be stated or left understood; the shorter way (Ang kumain…) is used more.
